summary.text:
Derbyshire Dales is a small district running as a NET INVESTOR. £5.5m of PWLB (one loan, PW492470, £5,450,000 at 4.10% maturing 2056) against £34.2m of treasury investments — net investor position of £26.5m at 31.12.25. Our price book reconciles exactly to Appendix B on rate and on principal. The £2.2m of finance leases is the balance of gross external debt at £7.7m; CFR is £7.7m and drifts down to £7.0m by 31.3.29 (Table 1).

The council's own liability benchmark (Table 2, p.5) turns NEGATIVE from 31.3.27 — meaning that with a £5m minimum year-end cash balance and a £2m liquidity allowance, no further external borrowing is required within the medium-term horizon. The existing £5.5m PWLB already sits SLIGHTLY ABOVE the loans CFR from 2026/27 onwards (over-borrowed by £0.1m–£0.4m across the window). Para 1.7 confirms no new borrowing planned for 2026/27; the £9m authorised limit is headroom for possible pre-funding, not a stated intention.

On the investment side, £24m of the £34.2m — 70% of the treasury book — is out to other local authorities. That's the largest single sector concentration in the book and puts Derbyshire Dales firmly on the lender side of the intra-LA market, alongside Chichester (£51m at 62%) and Basingstoke and Deane (£40m). Investment income budget for 2026/27 is £500k on a £15m average portfolio at 3.4% (para 2.50). Debt interest budget is £225,150 on £5.45m at 4.1% (para 7.1) — treasury is a net contributor to the General Fund by c.£275k.

Paper is small but self-contained. All treasury figures are inside doc 15465; no need to open the companion Capital & Investment Strategy (doc 15468) or MRP Policy (doc 15469) for the treasury picture. Report authorised by Karen Henriksen (Director of Resources / S.151 Officer) on 24 February 2026.

officer.body:
Hi Karen,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the Treasury Management Strategy that went to Council on 5 March. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first, which comes out cleanly. Our PWLB price book returns one loan for Derbyshire Dales: PW492470, £5,450,000 at 4.10% maturing September 2056. Appendix B on page 21 prints £5.5m at 4.1%. That's a full reconciliation — one loan, matching on rate to the basis point and on principal at your rounding, and it's the entirety of your external debt. Table 1's balance-sheet identity ties too: CFR of £7.7m minus £5.5m of borrowing minus £2.2m of leases lands on zero internal borrowing at 31 March 2025, drifting to £0.4m over-borrowed by 31 March 2029 as the leases amortise while the loan doesn't.

Where we can be more useful is on the other side of the book. Appendix B has £24m of your £34.2m out to other local authorities — 70% of the treasury book, and the largest single sector concentration in the portfolio. That puts Derbyshire Dales firmly on the lender side of the intra-LA market, and that market is the one nobody sees whole — every council sees its own trades and none sees where they sit against the sector. We track it across the library, so what other authorities are actually paying and offering for one-month, three-month, six-month and one-year money is visible rather than inferred. For context on the borrowing side, July's PWLB drawings were £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02% — a thin month, which shapes what deposit rates you're likely to be offered next. That breakdown is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

The other thing worth naming is what your own liability benchmark says next. Table 2 on page 5 turns negative from 31 March 2027 — the £5m minimum year-end cash balance plus the £2m liquidity allowance already put your existing £5.5m ahead of the loans CFR profile, and by 2029 the benchmark sits at minus £2.5m. Chart 1 makes the same point graphically. That reads as a settled long-term-investor position, which frames the 70% LA lending as a considered allocation rather than something driven by cash-flow pressure. The liability benchmark runs interactively on the live dashboard alongside CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard.

One data point from your Appendix A, which is worth a moment. Arlingclose's Central Case at 22 December 2025 had 5-year gilts at 3.85% for March 2026, which puts PWLB certainty around 4.65% at the medium end. Today's 5-year certainty rate is 5.34%, and the 10-year is 5.83% against a forecast 5.20% — roughly 0.6 to 0.7 percentage points higher across the medium tenors. Marginal to your position since paragraph 1.7 sets no borrowing plan for 2026/27, but relevant if the £9m authorised limit is ever activated for the forward-starting loans paragraph 1.10 keeps open.

On training, four fit. Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets is the most directly relevant given the shape of your book. Investment strategy for debt-free councils is written for the position you're effectively in — net investor by £26.5m with a small legacy loan running to 2056. Liability Benchmark: the essentials is worth watching given where CIPFA is heading with the codes. And Members' introduction to treasury is written for exactly the annual strategy cycle. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.
